title: Five ways to meet an attack
outcomes: Names the five ways to answer an attack (move, defend, capture, block, counterattack) and uses the first four to save a piece
Saves an attacked piece by a named way, and by any way when none is named
Checks that the chosen way still works against that attacker, and that it leaves nothing else loose
Says why defending fails against a cheaper attacker and why a far-away move is no answer

steps.text: That was one way to answer an attack. A piece is **attacked** when an enemy piece could capture it on the next move. When your attacked piece has no defender, you have five kinds of answer: **move** it, **defend** it, **capture** the attacker, **block** the line, or **counterattack**. You just used the first. Watch each of the others on a board, then try it.

steps.caption: White to move. The black rook attacks the knight on d4, and nothing defends it. First answer: move the knight. Nb3 is one safe square among several.

line.say: Move: the knight leaves the d-file, so the rook attacks nothing now.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing defends it.
One black piece, the rook, attacks the knight.
After Nb3 none of White's pieces is loose.
After Nb3 the engine line does not lose material.

steps.caption: Same position. Moving is not enough: the new square has to be safe. Look at the pawn on f7.

line.say: The knight lands on a square the f7 pawn attacks.
The pawn takes the knight, and White cannot take back. The knight was lost.

claims.statement: After Ne6 a black pawn attacks the knight on e6.
After Ne6 no white piece defends the knight on e6.
After Ne6 the engine line leaves White at least two points behind.

steps.text: To **defend** a piece is to put a friend where it could capture back. Then the attack is no longer free: if the enemy takes, you take back, and the trade decides. Use the counting values you learned. As a rule of thumb, defending works when the attacker is worth more than the piece it attacks. Count attackers against defenders too: two attackers beat one defender.

steps.caption: The first position again, second answer: defend. The rook goes to d1.

line.say: Defend: the rook on d1 now guards the knight along the d-file.
Suppose Black takes the knight anyway.
The rook takes back. Black gave a rook, worth five, for a knight, worth three.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing defends it.
After Rd1 one white piece, the rook, defends the knight on d4.
After Rd1 the engine line does not lose material.

steps.text: To **capture** the attacker is to remove the problem. First ask whether the attacker is defended. If it is, your capture starts a trade, so count it with the values. As a rule of thumb, capturing works best with a piece worth less than the attacker: a pawn that takes a knight wins the difference.

steps.caption: White to move. The black knight on e5 attacks the bishop on c4, and nothing defends the bishop. Third answer: capture the attacker.

line.say: Capture: the pawn takes the knight. The attack is gone, and the pawn is worth less than the knight.

claims.statement: The bishop on c4 is attacked and nothing defends it.
One black piece, the knight, attacks the bishop.
After dxe5 the engine line leaves White at least two points ahead.

steps.caption: A look-alike. The pawn on e5 attacks the bishop on d4, and taking it looks natural. Check what defends the pawn. (Moving the bishop, for example to c3, costs nothing.)

line.say: The bishop takes the pawn.
Another pawn takes the bishop back. White gave three points for one.

claims.statement: The bishop on d4 is attacked and nothing defends it.
One black piece, the pawn on d6, defends the pawn on e5.
After Bxe5 the engine line leaves White at least a point behind.
After Bc3 the engine line does not lose material.

steps.text: To **block** is to put a piece on a square between the attacker and your piece. It cuts the line, so it only works against a bishop, a rook or a queen. A knight jumps over pieces, and a pawn or king attacks the next square, so nothing can go in the way. The blocker is now in the line of fire, so check it is safe.

steps.caption: White to move. The black rook attacks the white rook on c1 along the open file, and nothing defends it. Fourth answer: block.

line.say: Block: the bishop steps between the rooks. The rook on c1 is not attacked now.
Suppose Black takes the blocker (not Black's best reply).
The rook takes back. Black gave a rook for a bishop.

claims.statement: The rook on c1 is attacked and nothing defends it.
After Bc2 no black piece attacks the rook on c1.
After Bc2 the rook on c1 defends the bishop on c2.
After Bc2 the engine line does not lose material.

steps.caption: A knight jumps, so you cannot block it. White to move: the black knight on b3 attacks the rook on a1, and nothing defends the rook.

line.say: Move with a threat: the rook leaves, and now attacks the knight.

claims.statement: The rook on a1 is attacked and nothing defends it.
One black piece, the knight, attacks the rook.
After Rb1 none of White's pieces is loose.
After Rb1 the rook attacks the knight on b3.
After Rb1 the engine line does not lose material.

steps.text: To **counterattack** is to ignore the threat and make a bigger one. It works when the piece that could take yours is also the only guard of your target, so taking drops the target. Ask: does the capture remove a defender of my target? Znosko-Borovsky argued [S, via synthesis sheet] that a counterattack needs a sound position, and that a half-measure is the worst choice.

steps.caption: White to move. The black rook attacks the bishop on c4, and nothing defends it. Fifth answer: counterattack. The rook can go to d1.

line.say: Counterattack: the rook attacks the black queen. Only the rook on c8 guards that queen, so if it takes the bishop, it drops the queen.
Black has to save the queen first (engine-checked, depth 16). The rook still eyes the bishop.
White has a move to spare and defends the bishop with a pawn.

claims.statement: The bishop on c4 is attacked and nothing defends it.
After Rd1 the rook attacks the queen on d8.
If Black then takes the bishop, the queen on d8 is attacked and nothing defends it (the pawn on b7 is loose too).
After Rd1 the engine line is close to level.

steps.caption: Same position, but White takes a pawn instead. The gain is smaller than the loss.

line.say: White takes a pawn. That is a threat, but a small one.
Black takes the bishop.
White takes a second pawn: two pawns for a bishop.

claims.statement: Rxa7 is a legal move.
After Rxa7 the engine line leaves White at least a point behind.

steps.text: Every answer must pass two checks. **Does it stop the attack?** Defending fails when the attacker is worth less than the piece (a rule of thumb): a pawn takes a defended knight and you lose a knight for a pawn. It also fails when attackers outnumber defenders. A far-away move does nothing. **Does it leave something else loose?** A piece that moves away can stop guarding a friend.

line.say: The bishop defends the knight, as the rook did before.
The pawn takes the knight anyway.
The bishop takes the pawn. White gave a knight, three points, for a pawn, one.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing defends it.
One black piece, the pawn, attacks the knight.

steps.caption: White to move. Two black rooks attack the knight on d4. One bishop defends it. Count: two attackers, one defender.

line.say: White trusts the one defender and plays elsewhere.
The first rook takes the knight.
The bishop takes the rook.
The second rook takes the bishop. White gave a knight and a bishop, six points, for a rook, five.

claims.statement: One white piece, the bishop, defends the knight on d4.
After h3 the engine line leaves White at least a point behind.

steps.caption: The first position once more. White ignores the attack and develops the bishop instead.

line.say: A bishop move to the edge. It does not move, defend or shield the knight.
The rook takes the knight.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing defends it.

steps.caption: White to move. The rook on d8 attacks the knight. The knight also guards the bishop on c2, which the rook on c8 attacks.

line.say: The knight runs away, and stops guarding the bishop.
The bishop is taken.

One black piece, the rook on c8, attacks the bishop on c2.
After Nb3 the bishop on c2 is loose.
After Nb3 the engine line leaves White at least two points behind.

steps.caption: Same position. Now the queen defends the knight, and the knight stays to guard the bishop.

line.say: The queen guards the knight and the bishop. Nothing is loose.

claims.statement: After Qe4 none of White's pieces is loose.
After Qe4 the queen defends the knight on d4.
After Qe4 the bishop on c2 has two defenders, the knight and the queen.
After Qe4 the engine line does not lose material.

steps.text: Edward Lasker warned, in *Chess Strategy*, that a defender can be an illusion [S, via synthesis sheet]: a cheaper piece may take it, a bigger threat may draw it away, or it may be pinned. [I] My broader reading: a defender can also be tied to another job, like the knight above. [H] My guess: the question "what else does it guard?" may catch many errors.

steps.caption: White to move. The rook attacks the knight, but the bishop defends it. Does White have to do anything about the knight?

line.say: No. The knight is attacked, but not in danger, so White plays a useful move elsewhere.
If Black takes anyway,
the bishop takes the rook. Black gave five for three.

One white piece defends the knight, so no white piece is loose.

line.say: The queen takes the pinner along the pin line, and gives check.

Qxb4 is a legal move.

steps.text: [H] A habit to try, not a law: list all five answers before you choose. Capturing and moving are the simplest. Defending needs a count. Blocking needs a bishop, rook or queen attacker. [I] In my reading, counterattacking is the riskiest, so check it last. Then run the two checks on your choice. Does the order matter? Our data cannot say yet, so test it on your own games.

[I] When two answers both work, prefer the one that does a second job: a retreat that eyes a target, or a block that also threatens something. This is my inference from the examples above, not a tested rule.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend, in your own words: they say "I will just defend my knight" against a pawn that attacks it. What do you tell them? Then tick what you included.

fields.label: The attacker is worth less than the knight, so the trade loses
Ask what else the defender guards

steps.text: **Compare.** An attacked piece can be moved, defended, saved by capturing the attacker, shielded by a block (only against a bishop, rook or queen), or saved by a bigger counter-threat. Before you choose, check two things: the answer really stops this attack, and it leaves nothing else loose. Defending fails against a cheaper attacker, and a far-away move is no answer.

steps.prompt: Think of a piece you lost lately. Which of the five answers did you check, and which did you forget? Did any answer you liked leave something else loose?

sources: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Part III: counterattack needs a sound position and weak points in the enemy camp, and a half-measure is the worst choice, paraphrased; sheet idea C23 (docs/citable-views.md 5.6) [V-sheet]

Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy: a defender can be an illusion (cheaper attacker, drawn away, pinned), paraphrased; sheet idea K3 (docs/citable-views.md 5.8) [V-sheet]. The 'tied to another job' wording is the author's broader reading [I]
